{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=strategies+for+autonomous+problem+prioritization+in+resource-constrained+systems&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Learning under constraints: a theoretical framework for comparing resource-constrained learning in biological and artificial systems.\", \"abstract\": \"Learning processes, cognitive architectures, available resources, and methods for sampling the environment and generating intelligent responses in complex sensory domains can differ significantly between natural and artificial systems. In this work, we present theoretical and modeling-based analysis of early-stage learning under resource constraints, comparing biological intelligence with a class of freely evolving, weakly constrained artificial systems (FEW), focusing on essential resource constraints such as computational capacity, memory, and energy. We develop quantitative models of sensory exploration and learning under strong and weak resource constraints, formalizing how limitations in energy, memory, and computational capacity shape sampling strategies and learning dynamics. For biologically constrained systems, we show that steep anisotropy in the cognitive cost gradient induces prioritized, depth-oriented exploration within limited sensory regions, leading to robust and resource-efficient learning. In contrast, we demonstrate that FEW systems, despite access to abundant resources, face a paradox of unconstrained learning: in the absence of intrinsic prioritization and evaluative feedback, uniform or random sampling leads to inefficient exploration of the sensory domain. To examine this challenge, we introduce a comparative framework for evaluating sensory traversal strategies and show that no single strategy dominates across prioritization accuracy, robustness, and resource efficiency. Instead, our analysis suggests a meta-strategy approach, in which adaptive selection among exploration strategies optimizes empirical success while preserving empirical accountability required for adaptive optimization. These results clarify the functional role of constraints in biological learning and provide principled guidance for the design of next-generation artificial learning systems operating in complex sensory environments.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fncom.2026.1636604\", \"pmid\": \"42388384\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13318973\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fncom.2026.1636604\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13318973\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13318973?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Autonomous AI research agents in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma immunology: from multimodal evidence to experimental validation.\", \"abstract\": \"Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most challenging malignancies due to profound biological heterogeneity, complex stromal organization, and limited responsiveness to current immunotherapies. Recent advances in single-cell sequencing, spatial omics, digital pathology, and multimodal profiling have revealed that PDAC immune states are shaped not only by cellular composition but also by spatial organization, treatment context, and patient-specific evolutionary trajectories. However, the increasing complexity and fragmentation of biomedical evidence create substantial challenges for conventional artificial intelligence (AI) approaches that are typically optimized for predefined analytical tasks. Autonomous AI research agents represent an emerging paradigm that extends beyond predictive modeling by integrating scientific reasoning, retrieval of heterogeneous biomedical knowledge, computational tool orchestration, workflow adaptation, and evidence traceability. In this Review, we examine how agentic AI systems may contribute to PDAC immunology research, from characterization of immune ecosystems and spatial cellular interactions to biomarker discovery, neoantigen prioritization, and experimental protocol design. We distinguish AI agents from conventional task-specific models and discuss essential capabilities required for reliable biomedical research, including planning, tool use, verification, memory, provenance tracking, and human oversight. Despite promising technical demonstrations in biomedical domains, direct evidence supporting fully autonomous AI-driven discovery and validation in PDAC remains limited. Therefore, we propose a disease-oriented evaluation framework emphasizing benchmark task design, appropriate human and computational comparators, reproducibility assessment, and experimental validation. Future PDAC-specific AI research agents should prioritize evidence-aware reasoning, multimodal integration, calibrated uncertainty, and transparent computational-experimental workflows. Such systems may ultimately accelerate mechanistic discovery and precision immunology, while maintaining rigorous standards for biological validity, reproducibility, and responsible scientific practice.\", \"doi\": \"10.3389/fimmu.2026.1983838\", \"pmid\": \"42921155\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13691739\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"Subscription required\", \"availabilityCode\": \"S\", \"documentStyle\": \"doi\", \"site\": \"DOI\", \"url\": \"https://doi.org/10.3389/fimmu.2026.1983838\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"html\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13691739\"}, {\"availability\": \"Open access\", \"availabilityCode\": \"OA\", \"documentStyle\": \"pdf\", \"site\": \"Europe_PMC\", \"url\": \"https://europepmc.org/articles/PMC13691739?pdf=render\"}]}}, {\"title\": \"Beyond the Algorithm: What Will It Take for Artificial Intelligence to Succeed in Indian Radiology?\", \"abstract\": \"Artificial intelligence (AI) is entering Indian radiology faster than the capacity of existing workflows to adapt, with increasing claims of expert-level algorithmic performance, a regulatory architecture beginning to form, and rising clinician interest. Yet translation of technically capable tools into reliable clinical value remains uneven. This perspective-style review synthesizes recent literature on radiology AI deployment, workflow integration, validation, and governance, with observations across public teaching hospitals, private diagnostic networks, and teleradiology settings. We argue that while the dominant discourse around medical AI remains algorithm-centric, the dominant problem in Indian radiology is workflow-centric. This mismatch is a major reason why promising tools often fail to deliver real-world value. We map the contemporary Indian radiology workflow, identify recurring structural bottlenecks, and locate the points at which AI can meaningfully augment clinical practice. We examine priority use cases according to clinical maturity, describe scenarios in which deployment may be unsafe or premature, and propose a staged departmental readiness framework aligned with India's emerging digital-health and AI-governance landscape. For radiologists, the article offers a practical way to evaluate AI tools against departmental realities. For administrators and policy stakeholders, it outlines a framework for institutional investment, validation, and governance. For developers and vendors, it clarifies where Indian clinical workflows may accept augmentation and where integration is likely to be difficult. Agentic AI systems are increasingly deployed in hospitals clinical decision support systems (CDSS), where multiple specialized agents negotiate over patient-care recommendations. This distributed negotiation introduced as “many hands” problem: overrides, disagreements and consensus-building can become opaque, and responsibility for erroneous outcomes cannot be clearly attributed. Existing healthcare AI ethics guidance largely address single system, output facing behavior and does not formally govern internal multi-agent negotiation. This study first synthesizes nine established game theoretic and mechanism design paradigms-including Prisoner's Dilemma, Bayesian games, signaling games, principal-agent theory, Stag Hunt, repeated games, VCG style mechanism design, Shapley value, and Chicken/Hawk-Dove mapping: their applicability and limitations for ethically accountable multi-agent CDSS negotiation. Building on this synthesis, we purpose the Musical Chairs Coalition Convergence Game (MC3G), a novel coalition-based framework that governs agent negotiation with a bounded protocol clock, a reputation-weighted convergence rule, and a mandatory escalation-to-human safety valve for any agent that fails to converge. As a proof-of-concept illustration of the framework’s qualitative behaviour rather than a clinically validated evaluation, we ran a synthetic simulation, non-inferential toy simulation (four agents, 2,000 cases per condition, varying strategic agent prevalence) comparing MC3G against naïve majority voting and reputation-only baseline. In this synthetic setting MC3G showed a lower silent failure rate alongside a higher human escalation rate, converting some undetected errors into flagged reviews. This offers a formally grounded, safety-first architecture for accountable multi-agent clinical decision-making, motivating future evaluation with real agents and data.
